- `idea`: its number.
- `about`: in Português Brasileiro, at most 60 characters: the question or topic the idea covers, so the learner knows what's coming without being told the answer. The learner reads it before the lesson, so it must not state the idea's conclusion, rule, definition, cause, number or verdict, and it must not paraphrase the idea's sentence. Write it as a short heading or question. For the idea "Net pay is what lands in your account after taxes and deductions", write how much of the salary the learner actually receives, written in Português Brasileiro; never that it's what's left after deductions.
- `icon`: every idea has one, and no two ideas share one. The map shows the ideas side by side so the learner can tell them apart, so each idea's icon must look different from every other idea's, not just have another name: two drawings of the same kind of thing (a cup and a mug) count as the same. When the ideas share a subject (the stages of one process, the kinds of one thing, a rule and its variant), at most one idea's icon shows that subject; every other idea gets the thing a learner connects with what sets it apart.

## For each screen

- `screen`: its number.
- `idea`: the number of the idea the screen teaches or asks about. A question that mixes two ideas takes the later one. Null when the screen covers several ideas at once and no single idea is about all of them, such as an overview of the whole process or a recap, since the learner would read it as being about one idea only; also null when the lesson has no ideas or the screen fits none of them.
- `underline`: only on an explanation or a worked example. The short phrase (2 to 10 words) that states the screen's main point, copied character for character from its text, without any `**` marks inside it. Null when no phrase stands out, when the main point is just the bold term, or when it would cover most of a sentence. Many screens have none.
- `example`: only on an explanation. The whole sentences that show a concrete case of the idea (a person, a number, an everyday situation), copied character for character with their `**` marks, from the start of a sentence to its final punctuation. Thaís afirma a Lorena que a OAB só pode cobrar rapidez da Justiça se também demonstrar que alguma lei foi aplicada incorretamente.
A afirmação de Thaís está correta?

Murilo diz a Lorena que, como a OAB atua com exclusividade na seleção de advogados, ela não pode defender direitos humanos de pessoas que não sejam advogadas.
Onde está o erro de Murilo?

Na sede da OAB, Sabrina analisa três pedidos: cobrar providências diante de violações de direitos humanos; promover a seleção de advogados; e assumir o julgamento de recursos atrasados.
Como esses pedidos se relacionam, nessa ordem, com as finalidades do art. 44 do Estatuto?

LESSON: Regra de três simples e composta

IDEAS:
1. Direta e inversa: Com equipe e ritmo fixos, o tempo cresce na mesma proporção que o pedido; para o mesmo pedido, mais trabalhadores no mesmo ritmo reduzem o tempo na proporção inversa.
2. Regra de três simples: A regra de três simples calcula um valor desconhecido usando duas quantidades relacionadas e uma condição fixa.
3. Regra de três composta: Na regra de três composta, o tempo inicial é multiplicado pela nova quantidade de etiquetas dividida pela inicial e pelo número inicial de impressoras dividido pelo novo.

SCREENS:

SCREEN 1 (explanation with its own picture)
O que fica fixo?
Na gráfica, Marília compara equipes e pedidos. Para o mesmo pedido, mais trabalhadores no mesmo ritmo reduzem o tempo na proporção inversa; com equipe e ritmo fixos, o tempo cresce na mesma proporção que o pedido. Essas relações são chamadas, respectivamente, de **inversa** e direta. Antes de comparar, diga o que permanece fixo.

SCREEN 2 (question)
Um carro mantém o mesmo consumo por quilômetro. Uma piscina é enchida por torneiras iguais, abertas ao mesmo tempo.
Como o combustível varia com a distância e o tempo de enchimento com o número de torneiras?

SCREEN 3 (explanation, may get an icon)
Uma mudança por vez
Marília também precisa pintar o muro da gráfica. Para o mesmo muro, se a equipe dobra e todos trabalham no mesmo ritmo, o tempo cai pela metade: a relação é inversa. Para calcular um valor desconhecido usando duas quantidades relacionadas e uma condição fixa, usamos a **regra de três simples**.

SCREEN 4 (worked example)
O prazo do muro
Quatro trabalhadores pintam o muro da gráfica em 6 dias. Em quantos dias 8 trabalhadores, no mesmo ritmo, pintam o mesmo muro?

SCREEN 5 (question)
Na gráfica de Marília, {printers} impressoras fazem {initial} etiquetas em {hours} horas. Elas mantêm o mesmo ritmo.
Quantas horas as mesmas impressoras levam para fazer {target} etiquetas?

SCREEN 6 (explanation, may get an icon)
Duas mudanças juntas
Marília muda tanto o pedido de etiquetas quanto o número de impressoras iguais, mantendo o ritmo de cada uma. Para achar o novo tempo, multiplique o tempo inicial pelo novo número de etiquetas dividido pelo inicial e pelo número inicial de impressoras dividido pelo novo. Esse cálculo é uma **regra de três composta**. A divisão das impressoras fica invertida porque mais impressoras reduzem o tempo.

SCREEN 7 (worked example)
Etiquetas e impressoras
Três impressoras iguais fazem 240 etiquetas em 4 horas. Quanto tempo 5 impressoras levam para fazer 600 etiquetas, no mesmo ritmo?

SCREEN 8 (question)
Na gráfica de Marília, {machines} máquinas iguais fazem {initial} peças em {hours} horas. Cada máquina mantém o mesmo ritmo.
Quantas horas {newMachines} máquinas levam para fazer {target} peças?

SCREEN 9 (question)
Numa padaria, {ovens} fornos iguais assam {initial} pães em {hours} horas. Cada forno mantém o mesmo ritmo.
Quantas horas {newOvens} fornos levam para assar {target} pães?

LESSON: Count with range() in Python

IDEAS:
1. Start and stop: In `range(start, stop)`, counting starts at the start and leaves out the stop, even when counting down.
2. Reach 5: `range(1, 6)` reaches 5 because it stops before 6.
3. Number of values: When counting up by ones, the number of values is stop minus start.

SCREENS:

SCREEN 1 (explanation with its own picture)
Stop before the end
Hannah’s `range(1, 5)` starts at 1 and gives 1, 2, 3, 4. In `range(start, stop)`, the stop is left out, even when counting down. To reach 5, use `range(1, 6)`. Counting up by ones, the number of values is stop minus start: 5 − 1 = 4. A loop over page numbers works the same way.

SCREEN 2 (question)
Hannah runs `for n in range(2, 6): print(n)`.
What does the loop print?

SCREEN 3 (question)
Hannah uses `for n in range(10, 0, -1): print(n)` for a timer countdown. The `-1` counts down by one.
What is the last number printed?

Naomi learns that one chamber sends blood to her whole body.
Which chamber does that job?

During Naomi’s heart exam, a doctor hears signs of a hole in the wall between her ventricles.
What is the wall, and why can a hole let blood mix?

LESSON: Particle in a box

IDEAS:
1. Boundary conditions: Infinite walls make the wave zero outside the box, so continuity gives $\psi(0)=\psi(L)=0$.
2. Allowed energies: The nonzero box states have $k_n=n\pi/L$ and $E_n=n^2h^2/(8mL^2)$ for positive integers $n$.
3. Standing waves: Each normalized standing wave fits $n$ half-wavelengths in the box and has $n-1$ interior nodes.
4. An electron's photon: An electron dropping from $n=2$ to $n=1$ in a $1.0\,\text{nm}$ box emits a photon near $1100\,\text{nm}$.

SCREENS:

SCREEN 1 (explanation with its own picture)
A box with walls
Naomi models a confined particle between $x=0$ and $x=L$. Its potential energy $V(x)$ is zero inside and infinite outside, where its wavefunction $\psi$, the particle's probability amplitude, is zero. Continuity makes $\psi(0)=\psi(L)=0$: these are **boundary conditions**, like a guitar string pinned at both ends.

SCREEN 2 (explanation, may get an icon)
The wave inside
Inside Naomi's box, the energy equation is $-(\hbar^2/2m)\psi''=E\psi$. Here $m$ is mass, $E$ is energy, $\hbar$ is Planck's constant divided by $2\pi$, and $\psi''$ is the second spatial derivative. With $k=\sqrt{2mE}/\hbar$, it becomes $\psi''=-k^2\psi$, so $\psi=A\sin kx+B\cos kx$. This oscillation resembles a vibrating string.

SCREEN 3 (question)
Naomi has $\psi=A\sin kx+B\cos kx$ inside the box and requires $\psi(0)=0$.
Which term can remain after she applies the condition at zero?

SCREEN 4 (worked example)
Allowed waves and energies
Naomi has applied the left boundary condition and found $\psi=A\sin kx$. Which values of $k$ and $E$ satisfy the right boundary?

SCREEN 5 (question)
Naomi considers assigning $n=0$ to the lowest state of the box.
Why must the lowest state instead have $n=1$?

SCREEN 6 (explanation with its own picture)
Waves that fit
Naomi sets the total probability in the box to one: $\int_0^L|\psi|^2dx=1$. This gives $A=\sqrt{2/L}$ and $\psi_n=\sqrt{2/L}\sin(n\pi x/L)$. Each **standing wave** fits $n$ half-wavelengths into $L$ and has $n-1$ interior nodes, points where the wave is zero. You prepare light marks for the screens of one lesson in a learning app. A designer turns them into an underline under a screen's main point, a frame around its example, a small icon beside the text, and a map of the lesson's ideas that the learner sees before and after the lesson. The text itself never changes: you only point at parts of it.

The input has the lesson's title, its IDEAS (the lesson map) and its SCREENS in order. Each screen says what kind it is.

## For each idea

- `idea`: its number.
- `about`: in Português Brasileiro, aiming for 60 characters or fewer: the question or topic the idea covers, so the learner knows what's coming without being told the answer. The learner reads it before the lesson, so it must not state the idea's conclusion, rule, definition, cause, number or verdict, and it must not paraphrase the idea's sentence. Write it as a short heading or question. For the idea "Net pay is what lands in your account after taxes and deductions", write how much of the salary the learner actually receives, written in Português Brasileiro; never that it's what's left after deductions.
- `icon`: every idea has one, and no two ideas share one. The map shows the ideas side by side so the learner can tell them apart, so each idea's icon must look different from every other idea's, not just have another name: two drawings of the same kind of thing (a cup and a mug) count as the same. When the ideas share a subject (the stages of one process, the kinds of one thing, a rule and its variant), at most one idea's icon shows that subject; every other idea gets the thing a learner connects with what sets it apart.

## For each screen

- `screen`: its number.
- `idea`: the number of the idea the screen teaches or asks about. A question that mixes two ideas takes the later one. An explanation or worked example that teaches several ideas at once with no single idea about all of them, such as an overview of the whole process or a recap, takes null, since the learner would read it as being about one idea only. Also null when the lesson has no ideas or the screen fits none of them.
- `underline`: only on an explanation or a worked example. The short phrase (2 to 10 words) that states the screen's main point, copied character for character from its text, without any `**` marks inside it. Null when no phrase stands out, when the main point is just the bold term, or when it would cover most of a sentence. Many screens have none.
- `example`: only on an explanation. The whole sentences that show a concrete case of the idea (a person, a number, an everyday situation), copied character for character with their `**` marks, from the start of a sentence to its final punctuation. Null when the screen has no such case or when the case is the screen's whole text.
- `icon`: only on a screen marked "may get an icon"; null on every other screen. Above the screen's text the learner already sees its idea's icon, so the screen's icon shows a different thing: the concrete thing of this screen's own case, such as the object in its example. The thing is named or described in the screen's text, never one you only associate with the topic. Never the same thing as its idea's icon, nor a variant of it. Null when the text names no such thing besides its idea's icon: no icon is better than one the learner can't connect to the text.

## Icons

An icon is a small drawing beside the text; the text carries the lesson.

- `name`: in English whatever the lesson's language, 1 to 3 words naming ONE concrete thing, lowercase and singular: an object, an animal, a plant, a place or a common symbol ("rubber stamp", "piggy bank", "balance scale"). Prefer a concrete object over a generic symbol; use a common symbol (law: balance scale; time: hourglass) only when nothing concrete fits. Avoid generic fillers (clipboard, document, folder, money bag, magnifying glass, lightbulb, question mark, checkmark) unless the screen is about that object.
- Name something the lesson's learner recognizes at a glance, never a part only an expert would know.
- Icons are shared by every lesson, so name generic things only: never a person, a face, a feeling, a brand or logo, a named place, letters, words or numbers.
- The same thing keeps the same name across the whole lesson.
- `searchWords`: up to 5 more English words to look the icon up by: synonyms and the thing's category.
- `description`: one short English sentence on what the drawing shows ("A wooden rubber stamp over a red ink pad"). Describe the thing itself, never an amount, a currency, a written label or anything tied to one country: the same drawing serves lessons in every language.

SCREEN 1 (explanation with its own picture)
Uma unidade minúscula
A água e outras matérias são feitas de unidades minúsculas. Elas se chamam **átomos**. O hidrogênio é um tipo de átomo.

SCREEN 2 (guess)
Quando dois átomos de hidrogênio se unem para formar o gás, o que acontece?

Os centros ficam separados

Regiões de energia

Elétrons mais externos

Contando no magnésio

Uma camada só

Átomos unidos
